title: Top 50 React Interview Questions & Mock Exam Prep
subtitle: Essential Q&A bank with self-assessment checks for complete React.js interview revision

chapters.title: Complete Interview Questions & Answer Bank
chapters.summary: Full collection of 50 essential React interview questions, key takeaways, and self-assessment checks.

sections.title: Q1: What is the Virtual DOM and how does React use it?
sections.content: The Virtual DOM is a lightweight in-memory representation of the real DOM. When state changes occur, React creates a new Virtual DOM tree, compares it with the previous one using a diffing algorithm (Reconciliation), and batch updates only the changed elements in the real DOM for optimal performance.
keyTakeaways: Virtual DOM minimizes direct real DOM manipulations to boost rendering performance.
React uses a diffing algorithm during Reconciliation to compute minimal real DOM updates.

interactiveQuiz.question: What process does React use to compare the new Virtual DOM with the previous one?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Reconciliation is React's algorithm for comparing two Virtual DOM trees and determining what updates need to be made to the real DOM.

sections.title: Q2: What is JSX and why do we use it in React?
sections.content: JSX (JavaScript XML) is a syntax extension for JavaScript that allows developers to write HTML-like markup directly inside JavaScript files. Compilers like Babel transform JSX syntax into standard `React.createElement()` function calls at compile time.
keyTakeaways: JSX allows writing component structure and rendering logic in a visual, declarative syntax.
Babel transpiles JSX tags into standard `React.createElement()` function calls.

interactiveQuiz.question: What does JSX transpile to under the hood?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: JSX is syntactic sugar that compiles directly down to `React.createElement()` calls.

sections.title: Q3: What is the difference between State and Props in React?
sections.content: Props (short for properties) are read-only inputs passed from parent components to child components to configure them. State represents internal, dynamic data managed within a component that can change over time and triggers component re-renders when updated.
keyTakeaways: Props are immutable data passed down from parent components.
State is local component data managed dynamically that triggers re-renders on change.

interactiveQuiz.question: Which of the following describes Props accurately?
options: Mutable local data owned by the child component
Immutable data passed down from a parent component
Global state shared across all components automatically
Asynchronous storage stored in local storage
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Props are read-only properties passed from parent to child components.

sections.title: Q4: How does the useState Hook work?
sections.content: The `useState` hook allows functional components to manage local state. It accepts an initial state value as an argument and returns an array containing two elements: the current state value and a updater function to modify that state value.
keyTakeaways: `useState` returns an array with the current state and its setter function.
Calling the state setter function schedules a re-render of the component with updated values.

interactiveQuiz.question: What does the useState hook return?
options: An object containing state and dispatch
An array containing current state and a setter function
A Promise resolving to state data
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `useState()` returns `[currentState, setState]` as a tuple array.

sections.title: Q5: What is the useEffect Hook and how is its dependency array used?
sections.content: The `useEffect` hook enables functional components to perform side effects (like data fetching, subscriptions, or DOM mutations). Its behavior is controlled by a dependency array: omitting it runs every render, an empty array `[]` runs once on mount, and specifying dependencies `[dep]` runs when those values change.
keyTakeaways: `useEffect` encapsulates side-effect operations in functional components.
The dependency array dictates when the effect executes (mount, update, or unmount cleanup).

interactiveQuiz.question: When does a useEffect callback run if passed an empty dependency array []?
options: Only once after the initial component mount
Continuously on a background timer loop
Only when props are mutated directly
interactiveQuiz.explanation: An empty dependency array `[]` ensures the effect runs only once after the initial component mount.

sections.title: Q6: Why are keys important when rendering lists in React?
sections.content: Keys are unique string identifiers used by React to track which list items have changed, been added, or been removed. Proper keys enable efficient Reconciliation during Virtual DOM diffing. Using array indices as keys is discouraged for dynamic lists as it can lead to state bugs during reordering.
keyTakeaways: Keys help React identify elements uniquely during list diffing.
Stable, unique keys prevent incorrect state mapping during list reordering or deletions.

interactiveQuiz.question: Why is using array index as a key for dynamic lists considered bad practice?
options: It causes syntax errors during JSX compilation
It can cause incorrect UI rendering and state corruption when list items change order
Index keys disable CSS animations completely
Keys must strictly be numbers instead of string indices
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Using array indices as keys breaks element identity when items are added, removed, or reordered.

sections.title: Q7: What are the main phases of the React component lifecycle?
sections.content: The React lifecycle consists of three primary phases: Mounting (component creation and insertion into DOM), Updating (re-rendering due to state or props changes), and Unmounting (removal from DOM). Functional components handle these using hooks like `useEffect`.
keyTakeaways: Lifecycle phases: Mounting, Updating, and Unmounting.
Class lifecycle methods (`componentDidMount`, `componentWillUnmount`) map to `useEffect` in functional components.

interactiveQuiz.question: Which lifecycle cleanup method corresponds to returning a function from useEffect?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: The cleanup function returned inside `useEffect` runs right before unmounting or before re-running the effect.

sections.title: Q8: What is the React Context API and when should you use it?
sections.content: The Context API provides a way to pass data through the component tree without manually passing props at every level (prop drilling). It is ideal for global state like user authentication, theme settings, or language preferences.
keyTakeaways: Context solves prop drilling by exposing data globally to wrapped component subtrees.
Best used for broadcasted low-frequency updates like user sessions, themes, or locale.

interactiveQuiz.question: Which hook is used to consume values from a React Context in functional components?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: The `useContext()` hook accepts a Context object and returns its current context value.

sections.title: Q9: What is React.memo and how does it optimize performance?
sections.content: `React.memo` is a higher-order component that memoizes functional components. It skips re-rendering a component if its incoming props have not changed according to a shallow equality check.
keyTakeaways: `React.memo` prevents unnecessary re-renders of functional components when props remain identical.
Uses shallow comparison by default for prop diffing.

interactiveQuiz.question: What type of comparison does React.memo perform on props by default?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `React.memo` performs a shallow comparison of current and next props to decide whether to skip rendering.

sections.title: Q10: What is the difference between useCallback and useMemo?
sections.content: `useCallback` memoizes callback function instances across re-renders to maintain reference stability. `useMemo` memoizes the calculated result value of an expensive function call across re-renders.
keyTakeaways: `useCallback(fn, deps)` returns a memoized function instance.
`useMemo(() => value, deps)` returns a memoized calculated value.

interactiveQuiz.question: Which hook is specifically designed to memoize the computed return value of a heavy calculation?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `useMemo` caches the result of an expensive calculation between re-renders.

sections.title: Q11: What is the useRef hook and what are its main use cases?
sections.content: `useRef` returns a mutable object whose `.current` property persists across re-renders without causing a component re-render when mutated. Common uses include storing DOM element references and holding instance values.
keyTakeaways: Mutating `ref.current` does NOT trigger a component re-render.
Used to access underlying real DOM nodes or store persistent non-rendering values.

interactiveQuiz.question: What happens to the component UI when the .current property of a useRef object changes?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Updating `.current` on a ref is a silent mutation that does not trigger component re-rendering.

sections.title: Q12: What is the difference between Controlled and Uncontrolled components?
sections.content: Controlled components have form inputs whose value is driven entirely by React state via `value` and `onChange`. Uncontrolled components maintain input state within the real DOM itself, accessing values using refs.
keyTakeaways: Controlled components rely on React state as the single source of truth for input values.
Uncontrolled components store value state in the DOM and read values using refs.

interactiveQuiz.question: Which element property dictates a input as a Controlled Component in React?
options: value bound to React state with an onChange handler
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Binding `value` to state and handling updates via `onChange` creates a controlled component.

sections.title: Q13: What is React.Fragment and why is it useful?
sections.content: `React.Fragment` (or `<>...</>`) allows grouping a list of children elements without adding extra wrapper nodes (like `<div>`) to the real DOM, keeping DOM layout trees clean.
keyTakeaways: Groups child elements without adding unnecessary DOM wrapper nodes.
Can accept `key` props when using full `<React.Fragment key={id}>` syntax.

interactiveQuiz.question: What is the primary benefit of using React.Fragment over a standard div wrapper?
options: Prevents adding extra DOM element nodes into the document layout tree
Fragment components automatically execute async effects
Fragments allow rendering objects directly without conversion
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Fragments eliminate clutter in the DOM hierarchy by rendering children directly without wrapper tags.

sections.title: Q14: What is a Higher-Order Component (HOC) in React?
sections.content: A Higher-Order Component (HOC) is a pure function that takes a component as an argument and returns a new enhanced component. HOCs are used for reusing component logic across an application (e.g., `withRouter`, `connect`).
keyTakeaways: HOCs are design patterns for reusing component logic by wrapping components.
Follows functional composition: `const EnhancedComponent = hoc(WrappedComponent)`.

interactiveQuiz.question: What does a Higher-Order Component accept and return?
options: Accepts a component, returns a new enhanced component
Accepts JSX, returns a DOM Node
interactiveQuiz.explanation: An HOC takes a component as input and returns an augmented wrapper component.

sections.title: Q15: What are Custom Hooks and why would you write one?
sections.content: Custom Hooks are JavaScript functions whose names start with `use` and can call other React hooks. They allow extracting reusable stateful logic out of components into isolated functions for sharing across the application.
keyTakeaways: Custom hooks encapsulate reusable stateful behavior across components.
Must follow Hook naming rules (`usePrefix`) to allow static linting.

interactiveQuiz.question: What naming convention MUST Custom Hooks follow in React?
options: Must be written in PascalCase (e.g. FetchData)
interactiveQuiz.explanation: React enforces that custom hooks start with `use` so static linter tools can enforce rules of hooks.

sections.title: Q16: What are the two core Rules of Hooks in React?
sections.content: 1. Call hooks **only at the top level** of components/custom hooks (never inside loops, conditions, or nested functions). 2. Call hooks **only from React function components** or custom hooks.
keyTakeaways: Never call hooks conditionally or inside loops to guarantee hook invocation order.
Only call hooks from React function components or custom hooks.

interactiveQuiz.question: Why must hooks only be called at the top level of a function component?
options: To ensure React preserves state correctly across renders based on static call order
Because hooks return Promises that block rendering otherwise
To allow Babel to transpile hooks to class methods
Because conditional hooks cause infinite loop memory crashes instantly
interactiveQuiz.explanation: React relies on the exact invocation order of hooks on every render to associate state values correctly.

sections.title: Q17: What are Error Boundaries in React?
sections.content: Error Boundaries are React components that catch JavaScript errors anywhere in their child component tree, log those errors, and display a fallback UI instead of crashing the entire component tree.
keyTakeaways: Error boundaries catch rendering errors in child component subtrees.
Must be implemented using class components with `componentDidCatch` or `getDerivedStateFromError`.

interactiveQuiz.question: Which lifecycle method makes a class component an Error Boundary?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `componentDidCatch` (and `static getDerivedStateFromError`) defines a class as an Error Boundary.

sections.title: Q18: How do React.lazy and Suspense enable code splitting?
sections.content: `React.lazy()` allows dynamic imports of components as separate bundle chunks. `<Suspense>` wraps lazy components, rendering a fallback UI (like a loading spinner) while the JavaScript chunk is fetched.
keyTakeaways: `React.lazy()` defers loading component code until it is rendered.
`<Suspense fallback={<Spinner />}>` displays placeholder UI while lazy chunks load.

interactiveQuiz.question: Which component is required to wrap a React.lazy component to display a fallback loader?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `Suspense` handles rendering fallback loading UI while lazy components are fetched over network.

sections.title: Q19: What is Prop Drilling and how can it be avoided?
sections.content: Prop Drilling occurs when props are passed through multiple intermediate components that do not need them, simply to reach a deeply nested child. It can be avoided using React Context, component composition, or state management tools.
keyTakeaways: Prop drilling creates unnecessary component coupling down deep hierarchies.
Avoid via React Context, Redux/Zustand, or component composition techniques.

interactiveQuiz.question: Which design pattern helps avoid prop drilling without using external state libraries?
options: Component Composition (passing children or JSX slots)
Storing all state in global window variables
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Component composition (passing child elements or slots) avoids threading props through intermediate nodes.

sections.title: Q20: What are Synthetic Events in React?
sections.content: SyntheticEvent is React's cross-browser wrapper around the native browser DOM event. It provides a consistent interface across different browser implementations while delegating events at the root container for efficiency.
keyTakeaways: Normalizes event properties across all web browser environments.
Uses event delegation attached to the root root container element.

interactiveQuiz.question: Where does React attach event listeners to handle user events efficiently?
options: To every individual DOM element directly
To the root container element where the application is mounted
To Virtual DOM nodes inside V8 memory
interactiveQuiz.explanation: React uses event delegation, attaching top-level listeners to the root app container DOM element.

sections.title: Q21: When should you use useReducer instead of useState?
sections.content: `useReducer` is preferred over `useState` for complex state logic involving multiple sub-values, when next state depends on previous state, or when managing state transitions using Redux-style action dispatches.
keyTakeaways: `useReducer` manages complex or grouped state state machines via `(state, action) => newState`.
Improves maintainability by decoupling state updates from event handlers.

interactiveQuiz.question: What is the signature of the reducer function passed to useReducer?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Reducers are pure functions taking current state and an action object, returning the updated state.

sections.title: Q22: What does React.StrictMode do in development?
sections.content: `React.StrictMode` is a development tool for highlighting potential problems. It intentionally double-invokes render functions, state setters, and effect cleanup functions to help detect unintended side effects and deprecations.
keyTakeaways: `StrictMode` checks for unsafe lifecycles, deprecated APIs, and unexpected side-effects.
Double-invokes functions in development mode only (disabled in production builds).

interactiveQuiz.question: Why does React.StrictMode intentionally render components twice in development mode?
options: To stress test browser rendering frames
To detect impure side-effects and cleanup bugs during state/effect updates
To compile JSX into Web Workers
To clear local storage caches automatically
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Double rendering helps highlight impure logic and missing effect cleanup handlers early in development.

sections.title: Q23: What are React Portals and when are they used?
sections.content: Portals (`ReactDOM.createPortal`) provide a way to render children elements into a DOM node that exists outside the DOM hierarchy of the parent component, useful for modals, tooltips, and overlays.
keyTakeaways: Renders React elements into external DOM containers.
Preserves React event bubbling through the virtual React tree regardless of DOM parentage.

interactiveQuiz.question: Which method creates a React Portal?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `ReactDOM.createPortal(child, container)` mounts elements into specified DOM nodes.

sections.title: Q24: How does React diffing algorithm achieve O(n) complexity?
sections.content: React reduces standard $O(n^3)$ tree diffing to $O(n)$ by applying two heuristics: two elements of different types generate different trees, and lists of child elements are tracked using developer-provided `key` props.
keyTakeaways: Heuristic assumptions optimize diffing from cubic $O(n^3)$ to linear $O(n)$ time complexity.
Changing element types unmounts the old subtree completely and builds a new one.

interactiveQuiz.question: What happens in React diffing when an element changes its tag type from <div> to <section>?
options: React updates only changed attributes on the element
React unmounts the entire old <div> tree and mounts a new <section> tree
React converts section tags into div tags automatically
React throws an invalid markup warning
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Different element types force React to tear down the old DOM tree and build the new one from scratch.

sections.title: Q25: What is React Fiber and what problem did it solve?
sections.content: React Fiber is the re-implemented core algorithm introduced in React 16. It enables incremental rendering by splitting rendering work into chunk units (fibers) that can be paused, prioritized, aborted, or resumed.
keyTakeaways: Fiber allows pausing and prioritizing rendering work to avoid blocking main browser threads.
Enables smooth UI responsiveness and concurrent rendering features.

interactiveQuiz.question: What primary feature did React Fiber introduce over the old stack reconciler?
options: Asynchronous, pauseable, and prioritizable incremental rendering
Direct real DOM mutations without reconciliation
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Fiber enables splitting rendering tasks into prioritized, interruptible work units.

sections.title: Q26: What is Automatic Batching in React 18?
sections.content: Automatic batching groups multiple state updates together into a single re-render for better performance. React 18 automatically batches updates inside event handlers, promises, `setTimeout`, and native event handlers.
keyTakeaways: Groups multiple state updates into single re-renders to eliminate extra renders.
React 18 extends automatic batching everywhere (promises, timers, native handlers).

interactiveQuiz.question: How can you opt out of automatic batching in React 18 if immediate render is needed?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `ReactDOM.flushSync()` forces React to immediately flush state updates synchronously.

sections.title: Q27: What is the difference between useEffect and useLayoutEffect?
sections.content: `useEffect` runs asynchronously after browser paint. `useLayoutEffect` runs synchronously after all DOM mutations but **before** the browser paints screen updates, ideal for measuring DOM dimensions.
keyTakeaways: `useEffect` is non-blocking and executes after browser layout and paint.
`useLayoutEffect` fires synchronously before paint, preventing visual layout flickering.

interactiveQuiz.question: When should you prefer useLayoutEffect over useEffect?
options: When fetching remote REST API data
When making synchronous DOM measurements to prevent visible screen flicker
When registering global browser scroll listeners
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `useLayoutEffect` blocks painting, allowing DOM measurements and adjustments before visual updates occur.

sections.title: Q28: What is React.forwardRef and when is it necessary?
sections.content: `React.forwardRef` allows parent components to pass a `ref` through an intermediate child component down to an underlying real DOM element or child component node.
keyTakeaways: Forwards refs down component hierarchies to expose underlying DOM nodes.
Essential for reusable design system components requiring DOM focus/measurement.

interactiveQuiz.question: What parameters does a component wrapped in React.forwardRef receive?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Components wrapped in `forwardRef` accept `(props, ref)` as arguments.

sections.title: Q29: How do you extract form values using refs in uncontrolled forms?
sections.content: Attach a `ref` object to each input tag via `<input ref={inputRef} />`. Read values on submit using `inputRef.current.value` without updating React state on every keystroke.
keyTakeaways: Eliminates per-keystroke re-renders by skipping state bindings.
Access form values on demand via `ref.current.value` during submission.

interactiveQuiz.question: How do you access an input value in an uncontrolled component using useRef?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `inputRef.current` points to the real HTMLInputElement DOM node instance.

sections.title: Q30: What is the useId hook introduced in React 18?
sections.content: `useId` is a hook for generating unique ID strings that are stable across server-side and client-side rendering, preventing hydration mismatch warnings for accessibility attributes (`htmlFor`, `aria-describedby`).
keyTakeaways: Generates unique, deterministic IDs for accessibility attributes.
Guarantees matching ID strings between SSR and client hydration.

interactiveQuiz.question: What primary problem does the useId hook solve?
options: Prevents SSR and client-side hydration ID mismatches for accessibility labels
Generates cryptographically secure encryption salt strings
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `useId()` ensures matching accessibility label IDs during SSR and client hydration.

sections.title: Q31: What are React Server Components (RSC)?
sections.content: React Server Components run exclusively on the server to render UI, returning serialized Virtual DOM structures to the client. RSC reduces client bundle sizes by keeping heavy dependencies on the server.
keyTakeaways: Server Components execute exclusively on the server and do not ship JS to the client.
Client Components (`'use client'`) add interactivity and state capabilities.

interactiveQuiz.question: Which directive designates a file as a Client Component in modern React frameworks like Next.js?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: The `'use client'` directive marks a component boundary where client JS bundle code begins.

sections.title: Q32: What causes React Hydration Errors during Server-Side Rendering (SSR)?
sections.content: Hydration errors occur when the pre-rendered HTML sent by the server does not match the initial Virtual DOM tree generated by React on the client (e.g., using `window`, dynamic dates, or non-deterministic IDs).
keyTakeaways: Mismatch between server-generated HTML markup and client rendered tree causes hydration failures.
Avoid accessing browser-only globals (`window`, `localStorage`) during initial render.

interactiveQuiz.question: Which scenario commonly triggers a React SSR hydration mismatch warning?
options: Rendering a dynamic date string like Date.now() directly during render
Fetching data inside useEffect after mounting
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Rendering dynamic client data like `Date.now()` produces different values between server and client.

sections.title: Q33: What is the useDeferredValue hook used for?
sections.content: `useDeferredValue` accepts a value and returns a deferred copy of it that 'lags behind' during urgent updates, keeping UI text inputs responsive while heavy subtrees re-render in the background.
keyTakeaways: Defers updating non-urgent UI subtrees to prioritize input responsiveness.
Works similarly to debouncing/throttling but integrated directly with React's concurrent render scheduler.

interactiveQuiz.question: How does useDeferredValue differ from standard JavaScript debounce timers?
options: It integrates with React concurrent rendering, updating immediately as soon as main thread is free
It delays state changes for fixed millisecond timeouts strictly
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `useDeferredValue` adapts dynamically to device speed, updating non-urgent UI as soon as rendering permits.

sections.title: Q34: What is the useTransition hook and how does startTransition work?
sections.content: `useTransition` allows marking state updates as non-urgent transitions. Urgent updates (typing text) interrupt non-urgent transitions (filtering a 10,000 item list), keeping the input frame rate smooth.
keyTakeaways: `startTransition(() => setState())` marks updates as low-priority transitions.
Returns `[isPending, startTransition]` tuple to monitor background pending state.

interactiveQuiz.question: What is the boolean flag returned by the useTransition hook tuple?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `isPending` indicates whether a low-priority transition render is currently processing in the background.

sections.title: Q35: How does the <Profiler> component measure React rendering performance?
sections.content: The `<Profiler>` component wraps React subtrees to measure rendering performance metrics, invoking an `onRender` callback with details like render duration, commit time, and phase ('mount' or 'update').
keyTakeaways: Measures rendering cost and re-render frequencies programmatically.
Accepts `id` and `onRender` callback props.

interactiveQuiz.question: Which prop callback must be supplied to the React <Profiler> component?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `<Profiler id="app" onRender={callback}>` invokes `onRender` whenever the subtree commits updates.

sections.title: Q36: What is State Colocation in React application architecture?
sections.content: State Colocation is the practice of keeping state as close as possible to where it is actually used. Elevating state globally unnecessarily causes distant unrelated component trees to re-render.
keyTakeaways: Keep state localized to the nearest common ancestor that requires it.
Prevents global state pollution and eliminates widespread re-render cascades.

interactiveQuiz.question: What is the main performance benefit of state colocation?
options: Decreases initial JavaScript download bundle size
Restricts component re-renders strictly to the local sub-tree where state is needed
Disables Virtual DOM diffing for child components
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Colocating state prevents triggering top-level parent re-renders that ripple down entire application trees.

sections.title: Q37: What is React.cloneElement and why is it increasingly discouraged?
sections.content: `React.cloneElement()` creates a clone of a React element while merging new props into it. It is discouraged in modern React because it makes prop sources implicit and hard to trace compared to render props or context.
keyTakeaways: Clones a React element and injects additional props.
Discouraged in favor of component composition or Context patterns due to fragile prop overriding.

interactiveQuiz.question: Which modern design pattern is widely preferred over React.cloneElement?
options: Explicit render props or Context API wrapper components
Direct real DOM node modification via refs
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Render props and explicit child components provide transparent prop contracts compared to cloning.

sections.title: Q38: What is ReactDOM.flushSync and when should it be used?
sections.content: `ReactDOM.flushSync()` forces React to flush any pending state updates inside its callback synchronously, updating the real DOM immediately before the current JavaScript block completes.
keyTakeaways: Forces immediate synchronous DOM updates.
Use sparingly as it disrupts React performance batching optimizations.

interactiveQuiz.question: What is the primary effect of wrapping a state setter inside ReactDOM.flushSync()?
options: Defers state setter to next idle frame
Forces React to apply state updates and flush real DOM changes synchronously
Schedules updates inside a Web Worker thread
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `flushSync` forces React to purge queue updates and update real DOM elements immediately.

sections.title: Q39: What is the useImperativeHandle hook?
sections.content: `useImperativeHandle` customizes the instance value exposed to parent components when using a `ref`. It restricts which internal methods or properties parents can access rather than exposing full DOM nodes.
keyTakeaways: Customizes imperative ref handles exposed to parent components.
Must be paired with `React.forwardRef`.

interactiveQuiz.question: Which React function MUST be paired with useImperativeHandle to pass the custom handle back?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `useImperativeHandle(ref, createHandle)` requires `forwardRef` to attach custom handles.

sections.title: Q40: How does Event Bubbling work through React Portals?
sections.content: Even though a portal renders into an external DOM node, events fired inside a portal bubble up through the **React virtual component tree** hierarchy, NOT the real physical DOM tree hierarchy.
keyTakeaways: Events bubble according to the React Virtual DOM component tree, not physical DOM nodes.
Parent React components can capture events emitted by portaled children components.

interactiveQuiz.question: If a button inside a Portal triggers a click, which component catches the event as it bubbles up?
options: Its physical parent container in the real DOM node tree
Its parent component in the React Virtual DOM hierarchy tree
Events cannot bubble out of Portals
interactiveQuiz.explanation: React Synthetic Event bubbling follows the React component hierarchy structure regardless of portal DOM mounting points.

sections.title: Q41: What is a Stale Closure in React hooks and how do you fix it?
sections.content: A stale closure happens when a hook or effect captures state/prop variables from an earlier render cycle and fails to update because dependencies were omitted from the dependency array. Fix by including updated dependencies or using functional state updates (`setCount(prev => prev + 1)`).
keyTakeaways: Stale closures read outdated state values retained inside closed-over effect scopes.
Fix using accurate dependency arrays or functional updater callbacks.

interactiveQuiz.question: How can you safely update state based on previous state inside a timer without capturing stale closure values?
options: Pass a functional updater: setCount(prev => prev + 1)
Omit state setters from useEffect completely
Store state in global local storage
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Functional updaters (`prev => prev + 1`) receive the guaranteed fresh current state without depending on outer scope closures.

sections.title: Q42: What is ReactDOMServer and what methods does it offer?
sections.content: `ReactDOMServer` enables rendering React components to static markup strings or readable streams on Node.js servers using methods like `renderToString()`, `renderToPipeableStream()`, or `renderToStaticMarkup()`.
keyTakeaways: Generates static HTML string or stream output for server responses.
`renderToPipeableStream` supports modern streaming SSR with progressive HTML hydration.

interactiveQuiz.question: Which modern method is recommended for streaming SSR responses in Node.js environments?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `renderToPipeableStream()` is the modern streaming method supporting React 18 Suspense streaming features.

sections.title: Q43: Why avoid overusing Refs for component communication?
sections.content: Overusing refs breaks React's declarative data-flow paradigm, making component state changes side-effect driven and hard to trace. Standard props and callbacks should handle application data flow.
keyTakeaways: React favors a declarative top-down data flow architecture.
Reserve refs for imperative escape hatches like focus management, DOM measurement, or media playback.

interactiveQuiz.question: What is the primary design philosophy of React data flow?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: React relies on a predictable unidirectional top-down data flow from parents to children.

sections.title: Q44: How do memory leaks occur in React functional components and how do you prevent them?
sections.content: Memory leaks happen when asynchronous tasks (API fetches, event listeners, subscriptions, timers) complete after a component unmounts and attempt to update unmounted state. Prevent them using cleanup functions in `useEffect` or `AbortController`.
keyTakeaways: Uncleaned event listeners or pending promises mutating unmounted state cause memory leaks.
Clean up subscriptions and abort HTTP fetch requests inside effect return callbacks.

interactiveQuiz.question: What is the correct way to cancel an active fetch request inside useEffect on unmount?
options: Use AbortController and pass its signal to fetch, calling abort() in cleanup
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `AbortController` provides native browser cancellation signals passed directly to `fetch()`.

sections.title: Q45: What are Optimistic UI Updates in React applications?
sections.content: Optimistic updates immediately update local UI state to show expected successful operation results before receiving server confirmation. If the network request fails, local state rolls back to previous values.
keyTakeaways: Provides instant user feedback by updating UI assuming server operations succeed.
Requires state rollback mechanisms when background network operations fail.

interactiveQuiz.question: What must an application perform if an optimistically updated network request fails?
options: Roll back local state to the saved pre-update state snapshot
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Optimistic UI patterns require restoring state back to previous values if server execution errors out.

sections.title: Q46: How do state management libraries like Zustand/Redux integrate with React 18 efficiently?
sections.content: Modern external state libraries use `useSyncExternalStore` to subscribe to external stores. This hook prevents concurrent rendering slicing tearing issues where different UI components read different store versions during concurrent renders.
keyTakeaways: `useSyncExternalStore` provides safe concurrent subscriptions to external stores.
Eliminates UI tearing issues during asynchronous concurrent rendering.

interactiveQuiz.question: Which official hook introduced in React 18 safely connects external global state stores without UI tearing?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `useSyncExternalStore` allows external store libraries to remain synchronized during concurrent rendering.

sections.title: Q47: Why are memoized selectors (like Reselect) used with Redux or global state?
sections.content: Memoized selectors prevent unnecessary recalculations of derived state data and return stable reference outputs, preventing downstream child components from re-rendering when unrelated global state changes.
keyTakeaways: Calculates derived state only when input state arguments change.
Preserves reference stability to prevent unnecessary child component re-renders.

interactiveQuiz.question: What happens when a memoized selector is called with unchanged input state arguments?
options: It re-calculates the derivation from scratch
It returns the cached result without re-executing derivation logic
It throws an unhandled promise error
It dispatches an automatic reset action
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Selectors cache previous inputs and immediately return cached outputs if arguments are reference-equal.

sections.title: Q48: What is the primary philosophy of React Testing Library (RTL)?
sections.content: React Testing Library encourages testing components as users interact with them rather than testing internal implementation details (state, instance methods). 'The more your tests resemble the way your software is used, the more confidence they can give you.'
keyTakeaways: Focuses on testing visible UI output and user interactions rather than internal implementation details.
Prefers queries like `getByRole`, `getByText`, and `getByLabelText`.

interactiveQuiz.question: Which RTL query priority is recommended for selecting accessible form buttons in tests?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `getByRole('button', { name: /submit/i })` mimics how assistive technology and real users locate elements.

sections.title: Q49: What is the act() helper function in React testing?
sections.content: `act()` guarantees that all rendering updates, state changes, and effect side-effects completed before assertions run, preventing async state update warnings during unit testing.
keyTakeaways: Flushes all state updates and pending effects before test assertions execute.
React Testing Library wraps user interaction helpers (`userEvent`, `fireEvent`) in `act()` automatically.

interactiveQuiz.question: What warning does wrapping state triggering code in act() eliminate during testing?
options: Warning: An update to Component inside a test was not wrapped in act(...)
Warning: Memory leak detected in V8 heap
Warning: Missing key prop inside dynamic list
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Wrapping state triggers in `act()` ensures test assertions execute only after DOM renders complete.

sections.title: Q50: What is the React Compiler (formerly React Forget)?
sections.content: The React Compiler is an auto-memoizing compiler that analyzes JavaScript rules and automatically memoizes component structures and values at build time, eliminating the manual use of `useMemo`, `useCallback`, and `React.memo`.
keyTakeaways: Automatically memoizes components and values at build time.
Removes manual developer overhead of optimizing with `useMemo` and `useCallback`.

interactiveQuiz.question: What primary manual hooks does the React Compiler seek to automate away?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: The React Compiler automatically injects fine-grained memoization, eliminating manual `useMemo` and `useCallback` annotations.

sections.title: Q51: What is React's built-in `cache()` function and how is it used in Server Components?
sections.content: React's `cache()` function allows memoizing data fetching or computation per request cycle in React Server Components (RSC). When the same function is invoked multiple times with identical arguments within a single server request, `cache()` executes the function once and returns the cached result for subsequent calls, preventing duplicated network requests or database queries during rendering.
keyTakeaways: `cache()` deduplicates data fetches and heavy computations per server request cycle in RSC.
Scoped strictly to the duration of a single request, preventing cross-request data leaks.

interactiveQuiz.question: What scope does React's cache() function apply to when used inside Server Components?
options: Global persistent server memory across all users
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `cache()` memoizes values per individual server request, ensuring clean isolation between concurrent user sessions.

sections.title: Q52: What are Server Actions in React and how do they work with forms?
sections.content: Server Actions are asynchronous functions that execute on the server but can be invoked directly from both Server and Client Components. They allow performing data mutations without writing API routes manually. When passed to the `action` attribute of an HTML `<form>`, Server Actions support progressive enhancement, allowing form submissions to work even before client-side JavaScript has finished loading.
keyTakeaways: Server Actions execute server-side mutation logic directly from component handlers or forms.
Enables progressive enhancement, allowing HTML forms to function without client JS.

interactiveQuiz.question: Which directive marks an asynchronous function as a Server Action in React/Next.js?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Adding `'use server'` at the top of an async function or file designates it as an executable Server Action.

sections.title: Q53: What is the useFormStatus hook and how is it used during form submission?
sections.content: The `useFormStatus` hook provides status information about a parent `<form>` submission, such as whether a Server Action is currently pending (`pending`), the form `data`, `method`, and `action`. It must be called from a component rendered **inside** a `<form>` element to read the surrounding form's submission status.
keyTakeaways: Reads pending state and submission data of parent HTML form elements.
Must be called within a child component nested inside the target `<form>` tag.

interactiveQuiz.question: Where must a component using useFormStatus be placed to read form state accurately?
options: As a direct child component nested inside the <form> element
At the root App level outside all forms
In a separate Web Worker thread
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `useFormStatus` reads status from the nearest parent `<form>` ancestor in the React component tree.

sections.title: Q54: How does the useOptimistic hook simplify optimistic UI updates?
sections.content: `useOptimistic` is a React hook that allows showing an optimistic state immediately while an asynchronous action (such as a Server Action) is pending. It accepts the current state and an update function, returning the optimistic state alongside a dispatch function. Once the background action completes or errors out, React automatically resets to the true state.
keyTakeaways: Provides instant UI feedback during pending asynchronous actions.
Automatically reverts to true server state once the underlying promise resolves or rejects.

interactiveQuiz.question: What happens to the optimistic state returned by useOptimistic when the underlying async action completes?
options: It persists permanently in client local storage
React automatically replaces it with the actual confirmed state
The component throws a hydration mismatch error
The developer must manually invoke forceUpdate()
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `useOptimistic` manages temporary state that automatically syncs back to actual state upon action completion.

sections.title: Q55: What is the new `use` API in React and how does it handle Promises and Context?
sections.content: The `use` API is a React function that reads the value of a resource like a Promise or Context. Unlike standard hooks, `use` can be called conditionally and inside loops or conditionals. When called with a Promise, `use` suspends the component until the Promise resolves, integrating directly with `<Suspense>` boundaries.
keyTakeaways: `use(promise)` suspends the component until resolution, enabling direct Promise consumption in render.
Unlike traditional hooks, `use` can be invoked conditionally and inside loops.

interactiveQuiz.question: How does the `use` API differ from standard React hooks regarding invocation rules?
options: It must only be called in class lifecycle methods
It can be called conditionally and inside loops or if-statements
It cannot be used with Suspense boundaries
It can only execute inside Web Worker instances
interactiveQuiz.explanation: The `use` API breaks the top-level restriction of traditional hooks and can be called inside conditional blocks.

sections.title: Q56: What is the Activity (formerly Offscreen) component in React?
sections.content: The `<Activity>` component (previously known as Offscreen) enables hiding UI trees while preserving their state and DOM nodes. When marked mode `hidden`, React sets DOM visibility to hidden and lowers the priority of updates inside that tree, allowing instant state restoration when switching back without re-mounting.
keyTakeaways: Preserves component state and DOM nodes when hiding UI off-screen.
Enables instant tab or view switching without losing user state or re-executing mounts.

interactiveQuiz.question: What is the primary operational advantage of React's Activity (Offscreen) mechanism over conditional rendering ({show && <Child />})?
options: It unmounts components to reduce memory usage
It retains component local state and DOM elements in memory for instant re-appearance
It disables CSS animations across all parent nodes
It skips Virtual DOM creation entirely
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Conditional rendering unmounts and destroys state, whereas `<Activity>` retains state silently in background.

sections.title: Q57: What is the useActionState hook (formerly useFormState)?
sections.content: `useActionState` is a hook designed to update state based on the result of a form action or Server Action. It accepts a target action function and initial state, returning `[state, formAction, isPending]`. It simplifies handling form submission feedback, errors, and pending indicators.
keyTakeaways: Tracks return values and errors from async form actions.
Returns state, wrapped action trigger, and a pending boolean flag.

interactiveQuiz.question: What three items are returned in the tuple from the useActionState hook?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `useActionState` returns `[currentActionState, actionHandler, isPendingBoolean]`.

sections.title: Q58: What are React Taint APIs (taintUniqueValue / taintObjectReference) for security?
sections.content: React Taint APIs prevent sensitive data (like security tokens, private keys, or user credentials) from being accidentally passed from Server Components to Client Components. By calling `experimental_taintUniqueValue()` or `experimental_taintObjectReference()`, React throws a build or runtime error if marked data is serialized to the client.
keyTakeaways: Prevents sensitive server-only variables or objects from leaking into client JS bundles.
Throws explicit compilation or runtime errors if tainted values cross server-client boundaries.

interactiveQuiz.question: What happens if a server object marked with experimental_taintObjectReference is passed to a Client Component?
options: React logs a silent warning in DevTools
React throws an error and blocks serialization to the client
React automatically encrypts the object string
The object is converted into an empty string
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Taint APIs strictly throw errors if marked sensitive data structures attempt to cross into client boundary payloads.

sections.title: Q59: How does flushSync interact with browser microtask queues?
sections.content: `ReactDOM.flushSync()` forces React to immediately execute pending state updates and flush the associated DOM updates synchronously. Because it bypasses React's normal batching queue, it drains pending state microtasks immediately within the current call stack, making DOM measurements available instantly.
keyTakeaways: `flushSync()` forces synchronous DOM re-renders within the immediate call frame.
Should be used sparingly as frequent forced synchronous flushes degrade frame rates.

interactiveQuiz.question: What is a major performance drawback of calling flushSync repeatedly in rapid succession?
options: Causes browser layout thrashing and dropped frame rates
Corrupts Virtual DOM reconciliation memory keys
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Forcing immediate DOM layout calculation repeatedly blocks browser painting and causes layout thrashing.

sections.title: Q60: How does React 19 improve support for Custom Elements (Web Components)?
sections.content: React 19 seamlessly integrates with Web Components by passing properties correctly instead of treating everything as HTML attributes. Custom attributes are updated properly, event listeners attach directly to custom element events without requiring refs or synthetic event wrappers, and prop data types (objects, functions) pass natively.
keyTakeaways: Passes props as native properties on Custom Element DOM instances.
Dispatches and binds native Web Component custom events directly without wrappers.

interactiveQuiz.question: How does modern React handle custom event bindings on Web Components?
options: Binds event listeners directly to native custom events emitted by the element
Converts all events into standard onClick listeners
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Modern React handles Web Component custom event handlers natively without needing custom ref attachments.

sections.title: Q61: What syntactic simplification was made to React Context rendering in React 19?
sections.content: In React 19, developers can render `<Context>` directly as a provider instead of needing `<Context.Provider>`. For example, `<ThemeContext value="dark">` is fully valid, reducing boilerplate code while maintaining backward compatibility for `Context.Provider`.
keyTakeaways: `<Context value={val}>` can be rendered directly without `.Provider` notation.
Simplifies Context usage across functional component trees.

interactiveQuiz.question: Which JSX element syntax is valid for supplying Context values directly in React 19?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: React 19 allows using `<MyContext value={data}>` directly as a provider without needing `.Provider`.

sections.title: Q62: How does React 19 simplify passing `ref` down to functional components without forwardRef?
sections.content: React 19 allows passing `ref` as a standard prop directly to functional components (e.g., `<MyInput ref={inputRef} />`). The component receives `ref` alongside other props in its parameter list (`function MyInput({ ref, label })`), making `React.forwardRef` obsolete for standard component wrapping.
keyTakeaways: `ref` can be passed and read as a standard prop in functional components.
Eliminates the necessity for wrapping functional components in `React.forwardRef`.

interactiveQuiz.question: In React 19, how is a ref accessed inside a functional child component?
options: Received as a standard property inside the props object: ({ ref, ...props })
Requires wrapping the component in higher-order class decorators
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `ref` is available directly on the props argument, eliminating the need for `forwardRef` wrappers.

sections.title: Q63: How do async functions work inside startTransition in modern React?
sections.content: Modern React supports passing asynchronous functions directly to `startTransition(async () => { await updateData(); })`. React automatically marks the pending state (`isPending`) as `true` during the entire duration of the async operation and handles loading UI transitions seamlessly.
keyTakeaways: `startTransition` accepts async callbacks natively.
`isPending` remains true automatically throughout the awaited async operation.

interactiveQuiz.question: What happens to the isPending flag when an async callback is passed to startTransition?
options: It toggles true instantly and returns false before the promise resolves
It remains true throughout the entire duration until the awaited Promise resolves
It throws a synchronous call stack error
It must be toggled manually using useState
interactiveQuiz.explanation: React tracks the Promise returned by async transition callbacks, maintaining `isPending = true` until completion.

sections.title: Q64: How does React natively handle Document Metadata tags (<title>, <meta>, <link>)?
sections.content: React natively handles document metadata elements. Rendering tags like `<title>`, `<meta>`, and `<link>` anywhere inside a component tree automatically hoists them into the document `<head>`, ensuring proper SEO and social sharing without external libraries like React Helmet.
keyTakeaways: Metadata tags (`<title>`, `<meta>`, `<link>`) are automatically hoisted to `<head>`.
Eliminates dependencies on third-party metadata management packages.

interactiveQuiz.question: Where does React place rendered <title> and <meta> tags placed inside deeply nested components?
options: Inside the local child div element node
interactiveQuiz.explanation: React detects metadata elements and hoists them directly to the HTML `<head>` tag during rendering.

sections.title: Q65: What are Resource Preloading APIs in React (prefetchDNS, preconnect, preload, preinit)?
sections.content: React provides built-in resource preloading functions inside `react-dom` (`prefetchDNS`, `preconnect`, `preload`, `preinit`). Calling these functions inside components allows React to hoist resource hints into the document head, optimizing stylesheet, font, and script fetch priorities early.
keyTakeaways: Built-in resource loading utilities optimize network fetching priorities.
Functions like `preload()` and `preinit()` hoist asset tags into `<head>` dynamically.

interactiveQuiz.question: Which method from react-dom preloads and executes a script asset with high priority?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `preinit('script.js', { as: 'script' })` preloads and executes target scripts as early as possible.

sections.title: Q66: How do Ref Callbacks support cleanup functions in modern React?
sections.content: Ref callbacks (`<div ref={(node) => { ... }} />`) support returning a cleanup function. When the DOM node unmounts or changes, React executes the returned cleanup callback, mimicking the behavior of cleanup functions inside `useEffect` for precise element lifecycle management.
keyTakeaways: Ref callbacks can return explicit cleanup functions.
Runs cleanup automatically when the referenced DOM element unmounts or updates.

interactiveQuiz.question: When does a cleanup function returned from a Ref callback execute?
options: When the associated DOM element unmounts or the ref callback updates
Only when the browser window resizes
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Returning a function from a ref callback gives a cleanup hook when the DOM node detaches.

sections.title: Q67: How and when should suppressHydrationWarning be used?
sections.content: When rendering content that inevitably differs between server and client (e.g., a timestamp or localized user setting), adding `suppressHydrationWarning={true}` to a specific JSX tag suppresses hydration mismatch warnings for that element without silencing errors across the rest of the application.
keyTakeaways: Silences SSR hydration mismatch warnings for deliberate client-server text differences.
Applies only 1 level deep on the element attribute where it is specified.

interactiveQuiz.question: What is the scope of suppressHydrationWarning={true} when applied to a <div> element?
options: Applies strictly to that element's direct attributes and immediate text content
Suppresses warnings globally across all application components
Disables hydration reconciliation completely for the entire page
Forces client rendering to be skipped
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `suppressHydrationWarning` is shallow, muting warnings only for the target element.

sections.title: Q68: What is onUncaughtError and how does createRoot handle unhandled error options?
sections.content: Modern `ReactDOM.createRoot` options include explicit root error handlers: `onUncaughtError` (uncaught error during rendering), `onCaughtError` (errors caught by Error Boundaries), and `onRecoverableError` (errors React recovers from automatically). This allows centralized telemetry and error reporting.
keyTakeaways: Root options provide granular hooks for tracking application errors.
Distinguishes between boundary-caught errors, uncaught crashes, and recoverable errors.

interactiveQuiz.question: Which root callback option catches errors that were successfully handled by an Error Boundary?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `onCaughtError` logs errors that were intercepted and handled by an Error Boundary component.

sections.title: Q69: What types of data can be passed across the Server Component to Client Component serialization boundary?
sections.content: Props passed from Server Components to Client Components must be serializable over the wire (JSON-serializable primitives, objects, arrays, Blobs, Promises, FormData, and Server Actions). Functions (except Server Actions), class instances, and Symbol descriptors cannot be passed across this boundary.
keyTakeaways: Props crossing from Server to Client must be serializable.
Supports primitives, plain objects, Promises, Blobs, and Server Actions; standard JS functions are forbidden.

interactiveQuiz.question: Which value CANNOT be passed as a prop from a Server Component to a Client Component?
options: A standard synchronous client JavaScript event function
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Standard functions cannot be serialized across the server/client boundary (only marked Server Actions are supported).

sections.title: Q70: What is Tearing in concurrent rendering and how does useSyncExternalStore prevent it?
sections.content: Tearing occurs when a visual state update causes different components on screen to display different versions of data for the exact same state variable because a store update occurred mid-render during concurrent yielding. `useSyncExternalStore` forces synchronous reads during external store updates to guarantee consistency across all components.
keyTakeaways: Tearing causes visual UI inconsistencies when external store data mutates mid-render.
`useSyncExternalStore` guarantees consistent synchronous store snapshots during rendering.

interactiveQuiz.question: What visual defect is referred to as 'Tearing' in concurrent user interface rendering?
options: Components on screen rendering different visual states from the same store concurrently
CSS flexbox containers overflowing screen borders
Missing keys causing dynamic list crashes
Unbound input fields dropping user keystrokes
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Tearing describes UI inconsistency where parts of the screen display old store data while others render new store data.
